title: Weather forecasting and why nobody believes it

turns.speaker: Dale
turns.text: It said thirty per cent chance of rain and it rained, and everyone in the office said the forecast was wrong.

turns.speaker: Zainab
turns.text: Which it wasn't. Thirty per cent means it rains on roughly three of every ten days like that one.

turns.speaker: Marit
turns.text: The forecasts are actually extremely good now. A five-day forecast today is about as accurate as a one-day forecast was in the eighties.

turns.speaker: Dale
turns.text: That's a striking comparison. Why does nobody feel that?

turns.speaker: Marit
turns.text: Because people remember the one wrong Saturday and not the two hundred correct Tuesdays.

turns.speaker: Zainab
turns.text: And the probability gets communicated badly. Thirty per cent of what, over where, during which hours?

turns.speaker: Zainab
turns.text: Some services mean thirty per cent of the area gets rain, which is a completely different claim.

turns.speaker: Dale
turns.text: So the number is right and the sentence is ambiguous.

turns.speaker: Zainab
turns.text: There's a forecaster bias worth knowing too. They tend to over-predict rain slightly, because being caught out costs more reputationally than a dry warning.

turns.speaker: Dale
turns.text: Which people then notice and trust it less, so the bias makes the problem it was protecting against.

turns.speaker: Marit
turns.text: The apps made it worse by showing a single icon for a whole day.

turns.speaker: Zainab
turns.text: One cloud with rain on it, for twelve hours across forty miles.

points: A thirty per cent rain forecast followed by rain is wrongly judged as an error.
Zainab explains probabilistic forecasts refer to frequency across similar days.
Marit notes five-day forecasts now match the accuracy of one-day forecasts in the 1980s.
Public perception lags because people remember rare failures rather than routine successes.
Communication is ambiguous, as some services express probability as the proportion of an area receiving rain.
Forecasters slightly over-predict rain for reputational reasons, which erodes trust, and single daily icons in apps worsen the problem.
